blocks.text: “They devoured the spotted, counterfeit body with insane frenzy.” Hence Pollux: Ἔστι δὲ τοῖς ἐλάφοις τὸ χρῶμα ἐπίξανθον, κατάστικτον λευκοῖς γράμμασι· πλείω δὲ αἱ θήλειαι τὰ στίγματα ἔχουσι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἐλάφων οἱ νεβροί. [Esti de tois elaphois to chrōma epixanthon, katastikton leukois grammasi; pleiō de hai thēleiai ta stigmata echousi, kai malista tōn elaphōn hoi nebroi.] “The colour of deer is yellowish, marked with white lines; the females have more spots, and the fawns above all.” Thus from the words νέβρος [nebros] and νεβρὶς [nebris] the serpent tseboa, because of its spots, was first called νέβρισσα [nebrissa] (like a certain town of Spain); then, the word being corrupted, נפרזא nephriza, or (as they pronounce it today) nephreza. And so these three names of the same serpent come to the same thing: צבוע tseboa; ברדלס bardales, or πάρδαλις [pardalis]; and נפרזא nephriza, or νέβρισσα [nebrissa]. For all of them have this in common, that they mean “spotted serpent.” But the name צבוע tseboa has something peculiar to it, which must now be noted. Properly, צבוע tseboa among the Hebrews is the hyaena, itself also so called from its spots. For the hyaena’s
— — — ἔῤῥαπται δέμας αἰνὸν Κυανέαις ἑκάτερθεν ἐπίτριμα ταινίαισιν· [errhaptai demas ainon / Kyaneais hekaterthen epitrima tainiaisin]

— — — “grim hide over the whole body is thickly sprinkled on every side with dark-blue stripes.” [III, 179] So Oppian, Cynegetica book 3, line 274. Accordingly, a little further on, he calls them στικτὰς [stiktas], spotted. And just as the serpent tseboa is believed to alternate its sex, so too is the quadruped tseboa, that is, the hyaena. Since I have proved this with many arguments in the chapter On the hyaena ^{a)}, it will suffice here to cite the words of the same Oppian:
Θαῦμα δὲ καὶ τὸ δ᾽ ἄκουσα περὶ στικτῆσιν ὑαίνης, Ἄρσενα καὶ θήλειαν ἀμείβεσθαι λυκάβαντι· [Thauma de kai to d’ akousa peri stiktēsin hyainēs, / Arsena kai thēleian ameibesthai lykabanti]

“This marvel too I have heard about the spotted hyaenas: that male and female alternate every year.” Rightly, then, the serpent is called tseboa, that is, hyaena, since it has both these things in common with the hyaena: a spotted skin and the alternation of sex, observed above by the [col. 397] Hebrews. And for the same reasons this same serpent was called hyaena by the Greeks and the Egyptians. Gesner, on quadrupeds, under Hyaena, p. 556: “Aelian and Horus in the Hieroglyphics have reported that the hyaena, not the quadruped but the serpent, is by turns male and female.” He had evidently read in Aelian, Historia book 1, ch. 25: Τὴν ὕαιναν ὄφιν τῆτες μὲν ἄῤῥενα εἰ θεάσαιο, τὴν αὐτὴν ἐς νέωτα ὄψει θῆλυν δέ· [Tēn hyainan ophin tētes men arrhena ei theasaio, tēn autēn es neōta opsei thēlyn de] “If this year you see the hyaena serpent as a male, next year you will see the very same one as a female.” And in Horus, Hieroglyphica book 2, ch. 65: Ὕαιναν ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ ὅτε μὲν ἄῤῥην γίνεται, ὅτε δὲ θήλεια· [Hyainan ophin zōgraphousin; hautē gar hote men arrhēn ginetai, hote de thēleia] “They paint a hyaena serpent (to signify an inconstant man): for it is now male, now female.” So read the books that Gesner had consulted. But in our editions the word ὄφιν [ophin] is missing in both places, because the editors struck it out as superfluous. This seems to have been done on a bad precedent and without reason, since, besides the Greeks and Egyptians, the Hebrews too reckon צבעים tseboim, that is, hyaenas, among serpents, and ascribe to them the same alternation of sexes. In Horus and Aelian, therefore, the word ὄφις [ophis], wrongly deleted, must certainly be restored; and to the Hebrew Lexicons must be added the word צבוע tseboa, which means both the quadruped hyaena and the serpent hyaena. For my part, though, I regard as fable what the Hebrews, Greeks and Egyptians write, that either the one or the other changes its sex by turns ^{*)}.
